The purpose of this mini-midterm is to give you an experience taking a short midterm exam, to see the style of some 
questions on the November midterm and final exam and to get some feedback on your performance so far. There will be 
opportunities for you to review your exam with the teaching team during office hours after it is graded.
The mini-midterm will be written during your normal class time om Friday, Oct 9th  and you must write with your 
registered section.
The mini-midterm will be 45 minutes.
You are allowed one individually written double-sided 8.5” X 11” sheet of notes (handwritten or computer -
generated). Additional layers like Post-it notes are not permitted. Make sure to include your name and student number
This is an individual exam. Note: the November midterm will have a group component.
This will be all multiple-choice questions or true-false questions. Note: the November midterm will likely have a mixture 
of multiple choice and short written answers.
Questions must be answered on a bubble sheet. Answers on the question paper will not be graded.
The exam will cover all material up to protein structure and function.
Mini Midterm

Learning Objectives
• List or recognize the roles of proteins within and outside of cells
• Predict the effects of changing amino acids on protein structure, function and stability. To do this 
you will need to be able to:
• Draw the generic structure of an amino acid and identify the key functional groups.
• Recognize amino acid classes based on the hydrophilic or hydrophobic properties of their side chains (R -
groups).
• Identify a peptide bond between amino acyl residues in a polypeptide (i.e. be able to circle it on a 
structure).
• Recognize and identify the directionality of proteins and how it is determined.
• Describe the features or characteristics of each level of protein structure: primary, secondary, tertiary, and 
quaternary.
• Identify the level of protein structure for a given protein, amino acid sequence or scenario.
• Identify the covalent and non-covalent interactions that are important for different levels of protein 
structure.
• Recognize and identify the types of covalent and non-covalent interactions important for protein structure 
and function.
• Define protein denaturation and describe the effects of protein denaturation on structure and function.
• Interpret or make figures showing the effect of the environment (e.g. temperature or chemicals) on protein 
structure and function.
• Describe the spontaneous assembly and folding of proteins using the relative terms; stability, bond 
strength, spontaneous and entropy (i.e. the hydrophobic effect).

Learning Objectives
• Apply your knowledge of amino acid side chains, the hydrophobic effect 
and intramolecular interactions in proteins to predict the likely R-group 
properties of amino acids based on their location within a protein’s folded 
structure (i.e. interior vs. exterior)
• Apply your knowledge of amino acid side chains, the hydrophobic effect 
and noncovalent interactions to predict (C4) the likely R- group properties 
of amino acids that mediate interactions between the protein and the 
environment (e.g. water, other macromolecules, membranes etc).
• Describe allosteric changes in protein structure as a control mechanism to 
alter enzyme or protein activity.
• Recognize and describe the role of many proteins as enzymes
• Recognize that noncovalent interactions with other molecules, and covalent 
modifications, affect protein shape and therefore function
